en: Shi Dunlun’s *Jizhuan* (Collected Excerpts), Volumes 3–5:
The Three Grounds of With-Seeking-and-Examination and So Forth (Part 2a–3b). 1. Treatise Text, Chapter 4:
Among the objects of the nine grounds, these are divided into three. The first two grounds have completed the clarification of the essential nature of the objects. This...
The three stages beginning with "with vitarka and vicāra" constitute the objective aspect (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*),
because their objective aspects differ in being inferior or superior, and coarse or subtle;
this is the intended meaning.
Vitarka (applied thought) refers to seeking;
vicāra (sustained thought) refers to examining.
Whether it be volition or wisdom, the coarse stage of searching for an object is termed vitarka.
These two types [of mental factors] are called *vicāra* when they are in the state of subtle investigation regarding an object.
It is not the case that these two factors are associated within a single moment,
because their respective categories of coarseness and subtlety differ in terms of temporal sequence.
Now, based on the existence or non-existence of those dharmas, these three stages (bhūmi) are established;
this is what is meant by the "explanation of the names.
As for the "establishment of the essence of the stages":
The *Śāstra* provides three explanations.
The first states:
"These three stages are established as the 'mindless ground' (*acittika-bhūmi*) based on the two preceding and succeeding correspondences."
The first two stages are called the "stages with vitarka and vicāra" (*savitarkasavicārā bhūmi*).
Therefore, it is known that all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) in the lower stages are called the "stages without vitarka and vicāra" (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmi*).
The second master says:
These three are established in relation to the two types of detachment from desire.
Since this fascicle designates the stage free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*) by means of being detached from the defilements of applied and sustained thought,
it is known that the first and second stages are so named because they respectively possess those specific defilements.
The third is the correct principle (*nyāya*).
These three are established solely in terms of realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*),
as explained in this fascicle.
The desire realm and the first dhyāna, whether in a state of meditative concentration or as a birth-realm, are termed the "ground with vitarka and vicāra" and so forth;
thus, it is known that these are established solely in dependence upon realms and stages.
Therefore, the challenges and refutations directed at the previous master are all incorrect.
The commentary on that text is explained in its entirety as stated therein.
Question: In the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, Dharmapāla establishes three stages based on the departure from desire (*vairāgya*);
this is similar to the position of the second master refuted in the *Vyākhyā*.
How is this explained?
The commentary, in refuting the second master, states:
"For one who has already abandoned desire, the dharmas of the lower stages are termed 'without vitarka and vicāra,' and so forth."
For one who has not yet abandoned desire, the various dharmas of the higher stages should be termed "with vitarka and vicāra" and so forth;
by this, the fault of confusion would be established.
Master Ce (Cemeng) further provided an auxiliary refutation, saying: [and so on].
If the three stages were established based on the departure from desire (*vairāgya*),
then the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) and the fundamental state (*maula*)— being identical in terms of their bondage and liberation— would constitute a single stage,
which would entail the fault of confusion.
The commentary states:
The meaning of the treatise itself has two interpretations. One says:
The protector of the Dharma (Dharmapāla) adopts the second explanation as the correct principle;
thus, there is no fault in either case,
for the inferior follows from the superior.
Freedom from passion is called "without investigation" (*avitarka*) and so forth;
all that is superior is inferior to what lies below it.
That which has not yet abandoned [passion] is not "without investigation" and so forth.
Therefore, there is no fault as previously stated.
Furthermore, it is taught that there are two occasions for the abandonment of desire:
namely, the time of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the time of actual abandonment (*maulavairāgya*).
Now, the term "separation from desire" is spoken in reference to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
Therefore, one first becomes separated from applied thought (*vitarka*) and subsequently from sustained thought (*vicāra*);
thus, there is no fault in the latter [position].
Second, it is said that the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*’s use of the term "detachment from desire" differs from that in the *Vyākhyā*.
Why is this so? Because there are two kinds of desire:
first, the desire of affliction (*kleśa-kāma*).
This refers to greed, hatred, and so forth.
Second is the nature of desire (*chanda*).
This means that the phenomena of the nine stages are called "desire" in the sense that they do not mutually repel one another according to their respective natures within those stages.
The term "detachment" (*vairāgya*) is explained as the nature of all dharmas belonging to a higher stage that inherently loathes the lower stage.
As stated in [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] 56:

"Because those sentient beings are detached from discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) by their very nature, they are detached from that stage; thus, although that stage is called 'without discursive thought and without investigation' (*avitarkāvicārā*)."
Thereafter, even its manifestation would be without fault.
In the commentary, the second master maintains that, based on the absence of the desire for afflictions (*kleśa*), there are the aforementioned two faults.
The correct principle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* relies on the teaching that [consciousness] is devoid of the desire for self-nature; therefore, neither of the two faults applies.
Within this section of the main text, there are three parts.
First, the question.
Next is the brief response.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "How are the designations of the elements established?
and so forth, this is a detailed explanation of the preceding heading.
However, upon examining the flow of the preceding and following contexts, there are three types of verses.
The first is the general verse (*piṇḍārtha-gāthā*),
because it summarizes the major chapters, both general and specific.
The second is the intermediate verses (*madhyama-gāthā*).
This is because they restate the headings of the preceding chapters and then provide a detailed enumeration.
Furthermore, it is said that after the headings have been stated and enumerated, [the explanation follows].
He then restated the preceding meaning in a single verse,
which is also called the "Middle Verse.
The third is the "Final Verse."
The meanings of the various sections are explained;
because they are collectively summarized and concluded in a single verse,
[the following] provides a detailed explanation of the five sections.
The section on the initial realm has three parts:
first, the question;
second, the answer consisting of eight sections.
This will be explained in detail later.
First, within the establishment of the enumeration, there are two parts.
The first indicates those that fall within the realms and those that do not.
Subsequently, within this [treatise], the three lower realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are explained individually.
These range from those not included in the [three] realms of existence (*dhātu*) up to the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
Master Jing’s commentary states:

These refer to the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*), the path of provisions (*sambhāramārga*), the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*).
Such paths as these are able to lead toward *nirvāṇa*.
Because it is subsumed within the Truth of the Path,
it is called "skillful means.
The view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is called the "false body."
The five appropriated aggregates (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are immediately eliminated through their counteraction;
this is their cessation through analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and the cessation that is the principle of suchness (tathatā).
As for the term "the realm free from conceptual proliferation" (niṣprapañca-dhātu):
The untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are different from the seeds of verbal designation and conceptual proliferation; thus they are called "without conceptual proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*).
Master [Xuan]zang further explains:
The untainted realm free from conceptual proliferation refers to the nature of *tathatā*, because its essence is untainted and free from discrimination.
Regarding "whether it is meditative absorption or birth":
this refers to either attaining that absorption or being born therein.

In this context, because one is free from the principles of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), it is called the stage without applied or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*), and so forth.
The second master cited this in his commentary as proof:
"The provisional designations for all phenomena in the first dhyāna of the desire realm, which have not yet abandoned vitarka and vicāra, are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.

The provisional designations for all phenomena in the intermediate dhyāna, which have already abandoned the defilement of vitarka but have not yet abandoned vicāra, are called the stage without vitarka and with vicāra only."
All dharmas from the two meditative attainments upward that are conventional and have already abandoned defilement are collectively termed the stage without vitarka and without vicāra;
this specifically indicates the distinctions such as instruction within the desire realm.
If it were already free from desire, it would also be called a stage without vitarka and vicāra;
however, this is not the actual meaning.
These three are established solely on the basis of the realms and stages.
This means that within the collection of both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are found;
all dharmas, whether already free from desire or not yet free from desire, are termed "equipoise" (*samāhita*) of that stage.
The preceding passage serves as proof:
it is not the case that a stage is designated as "that stage" simply because one possesses attachment to it, nor is it designated as "not that stage" once one has become free from such attachment.
To interpret it in this way would lead to great confusion.
Therefore, the treatise states:

"If the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) is included within the conditioned meditative absorptions, even the first dhyāna is called the stage with vitarka and vicāra (savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi), and so forth.
If the distinctions between the three stages are established based on association (samprayoga) and freedom from desire (vairāgya)."
All of these passages contain errors,
as explained at length in the *Vyākhyā*.
Regarding the statement that this is called the "stage without applied or sustained thought" (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*) because it is free from desire for applied and sustained thought:
However, it is taught that from those two meditative attainments upward, there is a single stage— both contaminated and uncontaminated— that is without vitarka and vicāra,
because in those attainments one is free from the defilement of vitarka and vicāra;
this is not the case for the lower stages.
One cannot claim that because being free from defilement constitutes that stage, the absence of defilement must therefore not be the case [in lower stages].
Thus, it is said that this applies only from those two meditative absorptions upward.
For this reason, the two lower stages are not mentioned; for in those stages, one ceases to belong to that stage as soon as one becomes free from its specific defilements.
Regarding the instruction on mental attention (*manasikāra*):
it refers to abiding in the desire realm with a mind that is signless (*animitta*) and free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*).

As for emerging from that meditative absorption, although the body remains in the desire realm, one has already abandoned the desire for the first dhyāna and enters a state of concentration free from applied and sustained thought.
When emerging from it later, vitarka and vicāra arise once again;
for those born in that [realm], even when they enter the second dhyāna and so forth, vitarka and vicāra of the lower stages still arise.
As for the statement that "the untainted realm is comprised within conditioned meditative absorptions," etc.:
For example, when non-conceptual wisdom arises based on the first dhyāna and takes true suchness as its object,
it is also called "wisdom of the stage with vitarka and vicāra," because this wisdom arises depending upon the stage of vitarka and vicāra.
It is not called "with vitarka and vicāra" because of the manifestation of discrimination associated with vitarka and vicāra;
for the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that at the time of realization, one is free from initial and sustained mental application (*vitarka-vicāra*) and conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, this stage is inexpressible.
If one relies on the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) arising from the first dhyāna to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, it is associated with vitarka and vicāra.
If there were no vitarka and vicāra, one would be unable to initiate the wind and produce speech to preach the Dharma.
Therefore, the first fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "The Bhagavat said:
'It is by relying on vitarka and vicāra that one utters speech.'"
It is not that they lack vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* asks:
"For what reason are the merits of mindfulness and wisdom of those with pure awakening not explained as being powerful within the various superior and sublime stages?"
The prose commentary states:
"Pure awakening is precisely the cause for the arising of verbal expression.
As for the phrase "the rest is as previously explained," it refers to what was stated before.
The preceding analysis is called the "stage without applied and sustained thought" (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*) because it is free from applied and sustained thought by way of having abandoned them;
it is not called "without applied and sustained thought" simply because the mind belonging to the stage with applied and sustained thought does not function there.
One should know that it is called the stage with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*) because one has not yet abandoned applied and sustained thought;
it is not designated as the stage with applied and sustained thought merely because one does not practice a mind that is without applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*).
Regarding the second location,
concerning the statement that "thirty-two thousand yojanas from here down reaches the Reviving Hell and the others," Master Ji provides the following explanation.
The meaning of this passage is as follows:
thirty-two thousand yojanas beneath the level of the earth one reaches the Saṃjīva [Hell];
the Saṃjīva is ten thousand yojanas in extent.
Descending further by four thousand yojanas from there, one reaches the Black Rope (Kālasūtra) Hell;
descending another two thousand yojanas from the Black Rope, one reaches the Crushing (Saṃghāta) Hell.
Thus, each of these eight hells is ten thousand yojanas in extent.
The distance between each of the lower six hells is two thousand [yojanas].
From the bottom of the Avīci Hell to the level of the earth, the total distance is calculated to be one hundred twenty-eight thousand yojanas.
Mount Sumeru enters the water to a depth of eighty thousand [yojanas].
This exceeds those [other hells] by forty-eight thousand [yojanas].
By this standard, it should be understood that the eight hot hells are deeper than the *Abhidharmakośa* [states].
They say that the level ground at the bottom of the abyss extends forty thousand yojanas;
they further state that although the water wheel is eight hundred million [yojanas] deep,
it rests upon the wind wheel.
The gold wheel is further three hundred and twenty million [yojanas] thick, resting upon the water wheel;
thus Mount Sumeru rests upon that gold wheel.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, the gold is beneath the water.
Next, it rests upon the golden wheel;
water is above the gold.
Although its depth is not explicitly stated, [it is understood to be one million yojanas].
Since the depth of the Avīci hell is calculated to be one hundred twenty-eight thousand yojanas,
yet it is stated that Sumeru enters the water by only eighty thousand,
it is clear that Sumeru does not rest upon the Golden Wheel.
It floats in the water, with half above and half below.
Master Bei (Baizhang) explained:
"Now, I rely on this treatise."
Each of the eight upper hells is four thousand yojanas high;
therefore, from this continent to the top of the Saṃjīva hell, there are thirty-two thousand yojanas.
The lowest [hell] occupies four thousand yojanas;
the remaining seven hells are situated below it, each occupying four thousand.
Thus, eight sets of four thousand amount to thirty-two thousand yojanas in total.
From the Reviving Hell upward, there are another thirty-two thousand yojanas;
together, this totals sixty-four thousand yojanas.
Yet, sixteen thousand yojanas still remain before reaching the Golden Ground.
The preceding text merely states that the various hells are ten thousand *yojanas* in width, without mentioning their vertical measurement; furthermore, each is four thousand [yojanas].
Therefore, the eight hells are each four thousand *yojanas* in height and ten thousand *yojanas* in breadth.
The eight hells are situated one above the other in vertical layers.
Furthermore, another interpretation states that since the masters of the treatises have established their vast dimensions as ten thousand [yojanas].
One should know that their height and breadth are likewise each ten thousand yojanas. Based on this,
one descends from this level ground for thirty-two thousand yojanas to reach the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.
The Saṃjīva Hell is ten thousand [yojanas] in length and breadth.
Below these ten thousand, there are seven other hells, each separated by more than four thousand [yojanas],
arranged horizontally rather than being stacked one above the other.
Why is this? Because from the level ground to the golden wheel it is only eighty thousand [yojanas] deep;
since thirty-two thousand have been subtracted from the top downward, only then do the eight hells exist.
There is only ground measuring forty-eight thousand yojanas;
how then can the eight hells, each ten thousand yojanas in height, be accommodated within it?
As it is with the Saṃjīva hell, so it is for the others as well.
Tài says: According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
these eight hells are established as being on the periphery of the eight great hot hells.
There is no other location.
The Saṃmitīya school says:
It is situated on the Iron Rim Mountains (Cakravāḍa), bordering the water-wheel and struck by cold air rather than by the light of the sun and moon.
Bei said: "Returning from the level ground, one passes downward through thirty-three thousand measures to reach the first cold hell.
From here, there is another interval of two thousand yojanas."
The seven hot hells are each two thousand [yojanas] in height, stacked one above the other.
Furthermore, it is explained that the eight cold hells are each ten thousand [yojanas] in both height and breadth.
From here, after descending thirty-two thousand leagues, there is the first cold hell;
further down, at an interval of two thousand yojanas, there are seven other cold hells situated around its perimeter.
The three states, such as burning and so forth,
are distinguished according to their being partial, more than partial, or complete.
As for a single aggregate (*piṇḍa*), its specific form is not perceived.
Because one perceives only the appearance of a mass of fire,
it is distinguished as being within the sphere of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Generally, there are three types of discourse concerning the cultivation of dhyāna.
First, there is that which is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), which perfumes the four lower meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).

Second, there is that which is exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), which pertains to the transformation death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward. Third, there is that which is both contaminated and uncontaminated.

For example, although the karma for the five Pure Abodes is created while one is still at the level of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), because it is now assisted by uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states that further support contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*), this karma causes one to be reborn in a superior realm.
Thus it is said: "Furthermore, there are those who transcend the Pure Abodes and attain birth therein."
Jingyun: Furthermore, above the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), there is the celestial palace of the Māra heaven;
thus, its location is described as being loftily superior.
However, this is subsumed under the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
Now, regarding the five Pure Abodes, it is stated directly that above them there is yet another place, surpassing the palaces of the Pure Abodes, where Mahādeva dwells.
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are born therein;
it is not said that they are subsumed within the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
This makes it clear that they are not subsumed under the [standard] stages (*bhūmi*).
Master Ji says:
This refers to the karma for rebirth in the Abhasvara Heaven (Bṛhatphala) created while still at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
When one is about to enter the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one is born in the Abhasvara Heaven.
The untainted (anāsrava) and most highly perfumed [karma] serves as the support for that prior karma of retribution;
it is only upon reaching the final mind of the tenth stage that one is born there.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
The benefit of present retribution consists in attaining the rank of a Buddha;
the benefit of future retribution consists in being born in the abode of wisdom of Maheśvara.
Regarding this term "born":
It is called "birth" because, through the refinement of coarse fruits, one attains increasingly superior and wondrous states;
there is no principle by which an outflow-free mind (anāsrava-citta) undergoes death or birth.
Regarding the four locations within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu):
There are four aggregates and faculties;
because the four voids differ in the length of their life spans,
they may have no location.
There are no separate palaces or dwellings,
because they are arranged at varying heights.
This is the third [point] regarding the dimensions of sentient beings.
Regarding the fact that the body size becomes increasingly taller and larger toward the northwest,
the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:
"The height of the people of Jambudvīpa is three and a half cubits or four cubits."
The inhabitants of the eastern, western, and northern continents increase twofold respectively.
It is said that on this continent [Jambudvīpa], they are either three and a half cubits or four cubits tall.
In the eastern continent it is eight cubits;
in the western continent, sixteen cubits;
and in the northern continent, thirty-two cubits.
Now, in this exposition of the vast [heavens], we do not speak of doubling;
because it is not fixed,
the Heaven of the Thirty-three increases by one foot.
This means that one *krośa* is divided into four parts; one of these parts is further divided into four parts,
and by adding this one part [to the original], it is called "one-quarter."
The Master further stated:
"There is yet another interpretation which says that 'one foot' refers to— "
A *krośa* is divided into four parts,
and each part is further divided into three;
because it constitutes one of these two [subdivisions], it is called "one foot" (*pāda*).
This indicates that the body of the Suyāma Heaven is one and a half krośas less half a krośa;
the body of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is one-third of a krośa;
and the body of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven is one-third of a krośa less half a krośa.
This differs from the *Abhidharmakośa*,
which states:
"In the desire-realm heavens, each [unit] increases by one-quarter of a *krośa*."
However, because the karmic fruits at the juncture of time, space, earth, and sky are difficult to overcome, they are equal to Śakra.
To explain this now:
Śakra dwells upon the summit of the terrestrial realm; his retributive reward is so preeminent that he is able to act in accordance with the divisions of time.
Question: Why is it that while the lifespan of the gods of the desire realm increases twofold, their bodies do not?
Answer: Because human life is the limit of what one can aspire to;
the body, however, is not so.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that beyond physical stature, there are many distinctions such as coarseness and subtlety, each with its respective gains and losses;
beyond lifespan, there is no other capacity.
Therefore, [the size] increases twofold in each successive stage.
As for the physical dimensions of the gods of the Form Realm, they are equal to those of the Heaven of Joyful Mind (*Tuṣita*).
The reason the physical dimension of Mahābrahmā does not increase twofold beyond that is as follows:
Because the karma of seeking the limits of existence and non-existence is difficult to overcome;
and because the three [stages] of the Cloudless [Heaven] involve the difficulty of cultivating meditative absorption while remaining free from the experience of change.
The bodies of those in the three evil destinies are indefinite as to their size;
they vary according to whether their karma is increased or diminished.
Thus, one should know that the physical dimensions of those in the Avīci hell are not necessarily eighty thousand yojanas.
However, there are sutras and treatises that state it is equal in extent to the entire hell;
this is said according to its maximum size.
Regarding the fourth point, the establishment of lifespan,
concerning whether the lifespans in the formless realms are doubled or not,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 84, states:
Question: For what reason do the lifespans in the formless realms increase by doubling, by half, or by a small portion?
Answer: Because the retributive cause possesses such power, one accordingly receives such a retributive fruit.
Furthermore, within the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, there are both infinite modes of activity and distinct modes of activity.
That is to say, the infinite mode of activity of the sphere of infinite space brings about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas.
The other modes of activity (*ākāra*) also bring about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas.
The mode of activity of "infinite" in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) brings about a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas;
the other modes of activity also bring about a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.
Above this, there are no further infinite modes of activity; there are only distinct modes of activity.
Therefore, their lifespan does not increase twofold as it does below.
However, in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there is a distinct superior wholesome contemplative practice that overcomes the notions of "self" and "mine."
This differs from other stages,
because that [wholesome karma] brings about a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas;
the lifespans brought about by other modes of action likewise increase twofold for each successive stage.
Furthermore, within the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, there are both śamatha and vipaśyanā.
That is to say, the śamatha of the sphere of infinite space brings about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas,
and the vipaśyanā likewise brings about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas.
In the two modes of practice within the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), each brings about a lifespan of twenty thousand years.
Above this, there is no superior wisdom, only meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
therefore, their lifespan does not increase further below that point.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, since none of the four formless stages possess manifold virtues,
the lifespan in the two [higher] meditative attainments is twenty thousand kalpas.
Because the three higher formless realms possess a small degree of detachment from the defilements of the lower stages, their lifespans increase twofold at each step.

That is to say, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), having already detached from the defilements of the single lower formless stage, brings about a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.
Adding the original twenty thousand to these, they constitute forty thousand kalpas.
Having abandoned the defilements of the two lower formless stages, one attains a lifespan of forty thousand kalpas in the Sphere of Nothingness;
adding the original twenty thousand to these, they constitute sixty thousand kalpas.
In the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, having abandoned the defilements of the three lower formless stages, one attains a lifespan of sixty thousand kalpas;
together with the original twenty thousand, this makes eighty thousand kalpas.
With the exception of Uttarakuru, in all other places there are those who die prematurely.
If the Hīnayāna teachings state that there is premature death throughout all three realms,
with the sole exception of those in Uttarakuru, the Heaven of No-Thought, and Bodhisattvas in their final body.
Although this present text does not explicitly state that Bodhisattvas in their final existence are free from untimely death,
it must logically be so; therefore,
the subsequent passage says:
Those who are neither harmed by themselves nor harmed by others include all hell-beings (*naraka*) up to Bodhisattvas in their final existence (*caramabhavika*).
However, regarding the Mahāyāna stage,
"Bodhisattvas in their final existence" refers mostly to the manifested aspect (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) rather than the actual final existence.
If one were to speak according to the actual facts,
those from the first bhūmi upward would have no untimely death;
why then need one go so far as to say that later-stage bodhisattvas have no untimely death?
Therefore, one should know that the statement in the following passage—that those Bodhisattvas in their final birth do not suffer premature death—is provisional and not ultimate;
for this reason, it is not discussed here.
As for the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva-deva):
According to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, there are three types:
if a weak cause brings about [rebirth], death will certainly occur prematurely;
if a middling karma brings it about, there may be premature death or there may not.
If superior karma induces rebirth without premature death, such fluctuations do not apply here; therefore, this is not discussed.
As for Uttarakuru, all there cultivate the practice of non-self-possessiveness (*anātman*), and since their attainment of the fruit is certain, they have no premature death.
Therefore, it is explained specifically here.
Within the fifth section on enjoyment (*paribhoga*), there are two parts.
First, three headings are presented.
This will be explained in detail later.
Within that detailed explanation, the experience of suffering and pleasure is clarified first.
The text is divided into four sections.

1. First, it clarifies that there is no pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) within the four types of hells (*naraka*). 2. Second, it clarifies that there is no pleasant sensation within the four types of hells, thereby explaining the presence of pleasant sensation elsewhere.
3. Third, it explains the distinctions between the excellence and inferiority of suffering and pleasure by means of six kinds of superiority.

Fourth, furthermore, regarding the physical basis upon which sentient beings of the three realms depend, he exhorts them below to feel weary of the three realms and to aspire to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Within the experience of suffering, this is further divided into two parts.
First, the suffering of the three realms is explained;
subsequently, that which is untainted and not suffering is explained.
Within the former, there are further two parts.
First, the suffering of the desire realm is explained;
subsequently, the suffering of the form and formless realms is distinguished.
Within the desire realm, two divisions are made.
First, the sufferings of the five destinies are briefly explained;
subsequently, the sufferings of the five destinies are explained in detail, beginning with the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).
Within this detailed explanation:
First, the suffering of the hells is explained.
The text is divided into four parts.
The first is the explanation of the great *naraka*s (hells).
Second, those near the border;
third, those in cold regions;
fourth, those who are solitary.
Regarding "the short *ṭa* near the edge of the middle [vowel]":
this refers to the excrement-and-urine worm (*gūthamūtrakiṭa*).
Because its snout is like a needle, it is called the "needle-mouthed" (*sūcimukha*) worm.
It is one foot in height, with a white body and a black head.
Regarding this insect, as well as the dogs, birds, and hell-wardens (*yamarakṣasa*), there are various differing traditions.
The masters of the Sarvāstivāda, the Sautrāntika, and the Mahāyāna maintain that these are non-sentient (*apudgala*).
However, there is a slight difference:
the masters of the Sthavira school maintain that it belongs to the category of sentient beings;
furthermore, they say that the Śālmali tree has the shape of a soapberry tree (*Gleditsia sinensis*).
Because it is filled with many thorns,
hell exists only beneath this continent.
If those from the other two continents who have severed their roots of goodness or committed an immediate offense come here to undergo suffering, [they do so because of this].
The *Vibhāṣā* states that all three continents possess both peripheral hells (*prādeśika-naraka*) and solitary hells (*eka-naraka*). Others say:
These two hells exist in the two continents [of Jambudvīpa and Pūrvavideha], but not in Uttarakuru,
because it is a place of pure bliss.
"Auspicious ones" refers to the Mañjuśrīs.
Regarding the flavor of *sudhā*:
among the gods there is a tree that produces the flavors of four kinds of food called *sudhā*,
which are blue, yellow, red, and white in color.
Regarding the statement, "Because the formless realm possesses afflictions and possesses hindrances," Master Ji explains:
Because it possesses afflictions, one lacks mastery over death; thus, death still occurs.
Because there is the obstacle of the "long-lived deva" difficulty (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva-vighna*), one lacks mastery over abiding in the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Now, this is explained:
it is by way of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and retribution (*vipāka*) that the meaning of being "incapable" (*akarmanya*) is revealed.
From here below, the second section clarifies the experience of pleasure, which is divided into three parts according to the distinctions of the three realms;
the first part is contained in this fascicle.
The latter two are in the fifth [aggregate].
Among the eight hot hells, the eight cold hells, the solitary hell, and the neighboring hells, there is no feeling of pleasure;
that is, there is neither ripening pleasure (*vipākaja-sukha*) nor pleasure resulting from outflow (*naiṣyandika-sukha*).

Regarding the statement that "the three types of hungry ghosts are likewise," it follows from what was previously stated regarding each of them that they are obstructed by external factors from obtaining food and drink;
this definitive analysis establishes that among these, there is no pleasure, referring specifically to the three types of ghosts.
Regarding the statement in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* that even a portion of animals (*tiryagyoni*) is called "pure suffering":
although this is indeed the case for animals, there is no distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) by which they could be specifically identified;
therefore, it is omitted and not mentioned.
Regarding the statement in Vasubandhu’s *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* that there is pleasure that is a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*),
the fifth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"It should be understood that this is spoken according to the principle of conforming transformation (*anuvartana*)."
This follows the explanation of the Sarvāstivādins and others;
or rather, it refers generally to other places of mixed sensation,
because there is no ripening pleasure (*vipākasukha*) and they are thus called "pure suffering."
Among the seven treasures, the wheel and the jewel are insentient;
the remaining five are sentient.
These two treasures, the wheel and the jewel, belong to Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
Below, he corresponds to a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).
The Elephant Treasure is one of the five hundred sons of the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita, who previously resided within the flank of the Asura.
The Horse Treasure is likewise the celestial dragon-horse of the Lord of Devas.
The queen and the two ministers were likewise subjects and attendants of the Lord of Devas.
When the Wheel-turning King’s transformation was exhausted, he died and returned to the heavens.
As for other kings, although they all possess the marks of a wheel-turner, [they do not fulfill the destiny].
There are distinct varieties of silver, copper,
and iron, but no other precious metals.
In the northern continent, those who have attained definitive progress are certain to advance further.
That continent necessarily possesses karma that results in rebirth in heaven as a subsequent retribution,
because prior to the contemplation of non-self, one cultivates the ten wholesome courses of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).
Thus it is stated in certain places.
He possesses karma to be experienced in a future life and will certainly fall among the hungry ghosts.
In the fifth fascicle of the *Śāstra*, the pleasure of the Form Realm is analyzed next;
regarding those who experience the joy and bliss born of seclusion in the First Dhyāna:
The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Mahāyāna), fascicle 2, states:
"Detachment refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained through the cultivation of remedies to sever the obstacles that are their opposites."
"Born" means that which is produced from this;
"joy" means...

That is to say, for one who has already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there is a feeling of mental joy, exultation, satisfaction, composure, and well-being, which is subsumed under the category of feeling (*vedanā*), based upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

"Pleasure" (*sukha*) refers to that which, for one who has already undergone the transformation of the basis, is based upon the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and is able to sustain the body as its support, causing the body to be joyful, satisfied, and at ease; this is also subsumed under the category of feeling.
Regarding the phrase "experiencing the joy and bliss born of concentration" in the second dhyāna:
"concentration" refers to the mind of one who has already undergone the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) abiding in a single object;
that is, the concentration previously attained.
"Born" refers to that which arises from meditative concentration;
its joy is as previously described.
It is not like the first dhyāna, where one first attains detachment for the very first time;
therefore, it is said to be "born of concentration.
Prior to the first dhyāna, there was no concentration.
Therefore, it is said only that [the feeling] is "free from birth" (viveka-ja) and not that it is "born of concentration" (samādhi-ja).
Regarding the statement that the feeling in the third dhyāna is "sublime bliss free from joy" (prīti-viveka-prasāda-sukha),
this refers to either taking as an object the teaching concerning the transcendence of desire for the second dhyāna.
Alternatively, having taken those instructions as an object, one perceives the faults in the signs of joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna and becomes weary of them.

"Sublime bliss" refers to the feeling (*vedanā*) categorized as a feeling of well-being, which is free from joy and free from elation, belonging to one who has undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
In this context, it is not said that "wonderful bliss is definitely produced" because one has just become free from joy (*prīti*).
As for the fourth dhyāna, its feeling is equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is pure, serene, and unshakable bliss.
Because they are free from the eight factors of grossness, defilement, and movement belonging to the two lower dhyānas: namely,
the first dhyāna is free from sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and the second dhyāna is free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), which are forms of suffering (*duḥkha*).
The third dhyāna is free from joy;
the fourth dhyāna is free from both pleasure and inhalation and exhalation;
therefore, it is called "tranquil and immovable."
Purity of equanimity refers to the state of transcending all movement within the lower three dhyānas— such as applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*),
joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*)— and thus abiding in the mind’s state of evenness, rectitude, and immovability.
Purity of mindfulness refers to the clarity of the mind that does not forget or lose its object, because it has transcended all such fluctuations.
These two are preeminent, which is why they are specifically mentioned here.
Below, the experience of the formless realm is distinguished:
it is the bliss of the liberation of ultimate tranquility.
In the sphere of infinite space, one is free from perceptions of form, ceases perceptions of resistance, and stills perceptions of diversity.
In the sphere of infinite consciousness, one is free from the perception of space and takes as its object the boundless consciousness of that sphere of infinite space.

In the sphere of nothingness, one is free from the perception of infinite consciousness; by searching for a further object beyond the sphere of infinite consciousness, one finds not even the slightest thing to be obtained, and thus excludes all that is non-existent.

In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having transcended the perception of nothingness and taking as its object a realm superior to the sphere of nothingness, one attains only the extremely subtle mind and mental factors of nothingness.
Because of this perception, it is called "extreme tranquility.
Because it is free from lower obstacles, it is called the "bliss of liberation.
The Abhidharma also states:
The maturation of tranquility exists because within that realm there is the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
because mental formations are subtle,
and because there is no matter produced by karma.
Because its duration is long,
it is called the bliss of peaceful liberation. This,
as well as the fourth dhyāna, receives the name "bliss" because it experiences physical and mental well-being.
Its essence is not the sensation of pleasure.

This concludes the first section. Next follows the second part, which generally clarifies the distinctions between the superiority and inferiority of suffering and pleasure; herein it is divided into three sections.
First, the excellence of the six sense bases is explained.
Next, the noble and non-noble riches are explained.
Following that, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, those who have desire for external objects" explains the distinctions in the suffering of experiencing sensory desires.
Within the section on the excellence of the six sense bases:
This indicates that from top to bottom, the hells possess increasingly distinct and intense sufferings.
Regarding the phrase "without discernment," it means that [the denizens] do not recognize their own karma and instead respond with anger toward the hell-wardens.
Regarding the phrase "because of successive delusions,
the instruments of suffering gradually increase," Jing says:
Unwholesome karma is the basis for the retribution of suffering;
it is called an "instrument of suffering.
Through the increase or decrease of karma, suffering likewise increases or decreases.
Now, let us explain.
"That upon which it relies" refers to the locus.
"Pleasure" is the opposite of suffering.
One who possesses discernment understands that present wholesome fruits are obtained through prior karma,
and by further cultivating wholesome deeds, the fruits of happiness increase.
If one were to say that happiness is obtained naturally by the self and not through prior karma, [it would be a misconception].
Since virtue gradually diminishes and pleasure quickly perishes,
it is not superior; this is the distinction between the noble and non-noble treasures.

Regarding the phrase "the wheel-stone and so forth without discursive thought" (*avitarka-cakra-pāṣāṇādi*): it means that there is no mind of analytical investigation or discursive thought (*vitarka*).
By means of revolving stones and hammers, one beats, strikes, and tramples the body, causing the body to grow.
This is the method of massage used in the Western lands.
Regarding items such as *śāntika* grass (kusha grass):
when practitioners of the Way in the Western lands travel, they carry these with them.
One should present the traveler with auspicious grass, or *bīṅgula* fruit, or a conch shell,
or a vessel filled to overflowing with goods;
by means of these auspicious objects, one manifests signs of good fortune.
It is called "pure requisites.
Regarding the *bimbi* fruit, it is the *bimba* fruit.
Jing says:
Its shape resembles that of a *karkaṭaka* fruit;
its interior is spongy,
and within it is like the color of *uragasāra* gold.
The essence of the seven noble riches (saptāryadhanāni) is, according to their respective natures, either contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Morality (śīla) and learning (śruta) are mostly contaminated;
relinquishment (tyāga) is, in fact, wisdom (prajñā).
Generosity may also be included within the category of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
These seven are established as the "noble riches" (*ārya-dhana*) because they are preeminent;
non-noble beings generally give rise to many [other] things that are contrary to these seven.
Within the section on distinctions,
because the pleasures of the three realms and the pleasure not bound [to them] constitute the noble wealth (ārya-dhana),
it should be understood by analogy from this.
The maturation within the three realms induced by various wholesome states, which is not conducive to the supramundane, is called non-noble wealth (*anārya-dhana*).
All wholesome states within the three realms as well as those that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) and conducive to the supramundane are all called noble wealth (*ārya-dhana*).
Regarding the fifteen kinds of distinctions:
the first ten consist of a single *ya* for each;
the first [of these] gives rise to both wholesome and unwholesome conduct.
Second, there is the presence or absence of fault;
"fault" refers to that which will result in an evil fruit.
Third, there is the pervasiveness or non-pervasiveness throughout the body.
The four seasons and their durations;
external conditions refer to material requisites,
while internal conditions refer to the sublime Dharma of the Noble Path.
Fifth, the breadth and narrowness;
sixth, the length and shortness;
seventh, the existence or non-existence of exhaustion.
Eighth, what is taken away and what is not taken away;
"taken away" refers to the encroachment and damage caused by the five families.
Ninth, what is maintained and what is not maintained.
"Fully sufficient" and "insufficient.
"Sufficient" refers to the fulfillment of the paths of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) of the three vehicles.
Under the character "again" (*yòu*) in the eleventh [section], there are five [points].
First, there is fear;
second, there are adversaries;
third, there are cross-currents of conflict.
Fourth, there is burning affliction;
fifth, one is unable to sever the great suffering of future lives.
Within the category of burning affliction, there is that which is like the disease of scabies.
Just as when one suffers from scabies, the extreme distress gives rise to a sense of pleasure;
though it is actually suffering,
one falsely conceives the notion of pleasure.
Worldly pleasures are likewise so.
Just as a leper experiences a false sensation of pleasure when his skin is bored by maggots,
so it is with wealth and status.
Regarding the distinctions among those who indulge in sensual desires, the text is divided into two parts.
First, the five virtues are set forth to demonstrate how the life of wisdom differs from defiled desire.
Second, from "Among these" onwards, the five faults are specifically revealed to distinguish [the life of wisdom].
Among these, the five faults are the opposites of the five virtues mentioned above, respectively.
First is defiled conduct;
to speak of equanimity without discernment is delusion.
Second, it is not ultimate,
because it is impermanent.
Third, it is not invariably fixed.
Because they share in mutual affection, mutual resentment, and so forth.
Fourth, there are those who do not fail [in their practice].
Those who live by wrong wisdom, although they have already become free from desire, fall back and give rise to it again.
The five are not real;
this is further indicated by the two instances of the word "also" (yu).
Among these, the first instance of "also" indicates that what is real is not [truly] real.
Furthermore, the subsequent mention of "names" refers to those who have not yet subdued Māra,
reiterating that [the names] are not real.
As for the term "Māra's army":
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the ten armies, such as desire and so forth,
refer to the activities of Māra;
that is to say, the performance of unwholesome karma.
From here below is the fourth [section], which exhorts one to feel weary of the three realms and to aspire to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that there is "delight in the flavor of existence" (*bhavāsvāda-rati*) and so forth, even down to those "subsumed under the two realms," there are two interpretations.
One interpretation states:
"The joy associated with relishing (āsvādana) belongs to the desire realm;

the joy dissociated from relishing refers to the joy associated with the pure meditative concentrations (śuddhaka-dhyāna) of the first and second dhyānas, specifically those belonging to the stages of decline (hānabhāgīya) or maintenance (sthityaṃśabhāgīya)."
That which possesses superior joy free from the savoring of craving is the joy associated with the stage of excellence and the stage of certainty;
these two belong solely to the realm of form and are subsumed within those two realms.
One interpretation states that within the many realms, three realms are taught: namely,
the realm of form (rūpadhātu), the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and the realm of cessation (nirodhadhātu).
Both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are collectively termed the "form realm.
Within this, there is joy associated with the craving for flavor (*āsvādanasamprayukta-prīti*), which is the joy associated with greed in the first two dhyānas of the desire realm;
and there is joy free from the craving for flavor, which is the non-defiled joy of the first two dhyānas of the desire realm.
The joy that is superior and free from attachment to flavor is subsumed within the untainted realm of abandonment (*anāsrava-prahāṇa-dhātu*).
The first two belong to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*),
while the latter one belongs to the realm of abandonment.
Therefore, it is said that they are subsumed within the two realms.
This refers to abiding in bliss, not to experiencing pleasure.
When entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the body becomes still and motionless; this is termed "abiding in bliss."
The first [section] clarifies the experience of suffering and pleasure;
the second concerns the experience of food and drink;
and [the third concerns] the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of those about to be born.
That which has already arisen is precisely the existence within the five destinies (*pañca-gati-bhava*).
It manifests the three realms (*traidhātuka*) without depending on the four kinds of nutriment (*catur-āhāra*).
This is stated in the fourth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
There are four kinds of nutriment.
The first is edible food, which has the characteristic of being subject to transformation and decay.
This means that the three— odor, flavor, and tangible objects— bound to the desire realm can serve as food at the time of transformation and decay.
For this reason, the sense-base of visible form is not included among the types of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*),
because visible form has no utility at the time of transformation and decay.
Second is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*), which has the characteristic of contacting objects.
This means that when tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*) first grasps an object, it can function as nutriment by appropriating joy and so forth.
Although this contact is associated with all consciousnesses, it belongs to the six consciousnesses.
The meaning of "nutriment" (āhāra) is predominant here,

because it excels in its ability to grasp and sustain the coarse and manifest objects, as well as joy, pleasure, and the beneficial equanimity that nourishes them. Third is the mental-nutriment of volition (manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra).
Aspiration is its characteristic.
This means that tainted volition (*cetanā*), operating in conjunction with desire, is able to perform the function of nutriment by aspiring toward desirable objects.
Although this volition is associated with all consciousnesses, it belongs specifically to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The meaning of "food" (āhāra) is predominant here,
because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) has a superior longing for its objects.
Fourth is the food of consciousness (vijñānāhāra).
Its characteristic is grasping.
This means that contaminated consciousness, through the power of increase by means of morsel food, contact, and volition, is able to function as nutriment.
Although this consciousness is common to the nature of all [eight] consciousnesses, the eighth consciousness is preeminent in the sense of being nutriment.
Because they excel in maintaining the continuity of a single class [of beings],
the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that these four nutriments are subsumed within three aggregates (*skandha*), five bases (*āyatana*), and eleven elements (*dhātu*).
Among these, edible food may consist solely of fragrance,
as is the case with the food consumed by those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); or it may consist solely of tangible contact.
For instance, the winds and so forth within the storehouse of the hells do not necessarily possess all three [characteristics].
Furthermore, regarding those who go to the hells and remain there for a long duration:
All the great hells possess this food.
While sixty-six [treatises] state that there is no coarse food,
here we speak of the subtle kind.
These subtle objects also exist in the minor hells;
for it is only when various types of solid food undergo transformation that they can perform their function of sustaining the sense faculties and so forth,
and by this causal condition, those beings are able to endure for a long time.
This is not like the Hīnayāna, which describes swallowing iron balls as "food" because they temporarily alleviate hunger and thirst;
according to the meaning of the Mahāyāna, the suffering of hunger and thirst is light,
whereas the suffering produced by molten iron balls is heavy.
Because the heavy [suffering] overcomes the light, they do not perceive hunger or thirst;
this does not mean that the iron balls and such are actually edible.
Third, regarding the enjoyment of sexual desire:
Regarding the absence of sexual activity in the *naraka*s (hells):
it is absent in all four types of hells. Some, however, say:
The eight cold and hot hells do not exist there;
only the solitary hell (pratyekanaraka) exists.
Question: Since the two heavens above [the desire realm] lack physical appropriation (upādāna), how can this be?
How can there be the courses of action consisting of taking what is not given and sexual misconduct?
Answer: They exist because there are those who transform [beings] without appropriating the fruits of their karma; thus, there are two courses of action.
Or if that [the cause] does not possess this [the effect], what difference does it make? Jing said:
In reality, the actual women belonging to those two devas still have owners;
it is just as when the twelve thousand celestial maidens in Vimalakīrti’s chamber returned to the palace with Māra.
Among them, whether the goddesses are emanations or real, or whether they possess no attachment,
how is it that they follow Māra back to their celestial palaces?
This is explained in the section on the establishment of the sixth birth.
Regarding the term "unshakable" (*āneñja*):
it is said because the fourth dhyāna is free from the sensation of change (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*).
This is the seventh self-entity (*ātma-bhāva*).
Regarding "those who sport with deluded thoughts" and "those who are enraged in mind," Master Jing and others explain that these are the four heavens dwelling in space within the Desire Realm.
The latter two heavens are both included within the category of "sentient beings" (sattva),
because they are not killed by non-gods (asura).
This was subsequently supplemented by a question.
When Śakra fought with the asuras,
the four heavens above each dispatched their celestial hosts to assist Śakra,
guarding the four sides of Mount Sumeru.
What does it mean to "not fight with the asuras"?
The explanation says:
it merely means assisting in the defense of the city, not engaging in combat with them.
If that is so, since the four heavens above do not harm themselves nor kill asuras,
they would have no karma of killing;
how then can there be ten unwholesome karmas among the gods of the desire realm?
The commentary states:
This is a general statement that the gods of the desire realm commit the ten unwholesome karmas;
it does not necessarily mean that all six heavens commit them universally.

Question: If this passage were to prove that the mental states of playful wandering, deluded thought, and mutual resentment pervade the four heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), why is it stated in the third chapter of the *Abhidharma* (*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*), among the twenty-four types of "already arisen" [beings], that they are not present there?
Regarding those who have already attained purity:
this refers to the playful delusions of the mental faculty, resentment, and hostility;

as well as the excessive negligence of the gods of the Realm of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*), the gods of the Realm of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), and the gods of the Form and Formless Realms.
Therefore, according to what is appropriate, they exercise mastery over the objects of enjoyment and the meditative absorptions in which they dwell.
Those that have already arisen but are not yet purified refer to the remainder thereof.
This passage explains that the name of the Yāma Heaven is "Sporting with Delusive Thoughts," while that of the Tuṣita Heaven is "Mutual Resentment of Mental Images.
This is followed by a specific clarification regarding the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmitavaśavartin Heavens.
Master Xuanzang’s commentary explains:
This statement was made in order to distinguish the four classes of gods who dwell in the air;
for the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations belongs exclusively to the sixth [dhyāna].
The Heaven of Delighting in Transformations belongs exclusively to the fifth [dhyāna].
Therefore, it is said that mental resentment belongs to the fourth heaven,
while playful delusions belong to the third heaven.

The gods who sport in principles (dharmārambaṇa-krīḍana), those with discursive thoughts (vitarka-vicāra), those with mental images (saṃjñin), those with mutual resentment (pratigha-saṃyojana), and those who dwell in the air (antarīkṣa) comprise the four classes of the heavens of the desire realm.
Among these, two classes of earth-dwelling gods (bhūmi-cara) engage in sexual desire in a manner similar to humans;
therefore, they are not designated as "purely born" (viśuddha-jāta).
The Four Heavens of the Sky-Dwellers merely embrace one another, hold hands, smile at one another, and gaze at one another;
their engagement in sexual desire is slight.
For this reason, they are named "Purely Born."
According to that *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
false thoughts and mental anger all pertain to the six desire realms (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara*).
Regarding the phrase "those sentient beings who are in the state of having already been born," and so forth:
Even though this does not apply to the stage of the *kalala*,
at the time of reaching the stage of having already been born, moisture-born, transformation-born, and so forth are all included in this statement;
however, following the preceding text, it is here said that they have already been born in their respective places of birth.
Regarding the "messenger of the Tathāgata among those who are neither [existent nor non-existent]," it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
when the mother of the householder Jyotiṣka was pregnant with Jyotiṣka...
The Buddha had prophesied that the child would be male; however, before the child was born, the mother passed away.
The non-Buddhists mocked and reviled the Buddha, claiming his prophecy was without fulfillment.
On the day the mother was cremated, the Buddha commanded a messenger to enter the fire and retrieve the child.
Although the mother had perished, the child did not die;
by the power of the Buddha, the fire did not consume him.
The Buddha predicted the survival of the child, but did not predict that of the mother.
Therefore, it is said that [this statement] is not false.
Question: The gods of the two upper realms also experience premature death;
why, then, is this not called "self-harm"?
Answer: For all sentient beings, indeterminate karma is generally exhausted through the depletion of merit;
therefore, they meet with premature death.
This is not the same as the gods of the desire realm, whose food arises frequently and whose superior mental states manifest continuously.
However, merely diminishing one's celestial retribution is termed "self-harm.
Regarding the eighth causal condition, there are two parts within the result:
first, the presentation of four gates; second, the detailed explanation according to each.
Within the analysis of characteristics, there are further two parts.
First, a general presentation enumerates five kinds of causal conditions and their resultant characteristics:
namely, those acquired at birth and those resulting from cultivation.
Hereafter, based on these five questions and answers, there is a detailed explanation.
Regarding the first gate within the section on birth, "What serves as the precursor?
is the question concerning the cause.
"Who establishes it and who brings it together?
asks regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*).
"What dharma arises? asks regarding the result.
This is a question concerning the fruit.
All subsequent questions are to be understood in this same manner.
"Is it preceded by its own seed? means:
Taking the熏習 (vāsanā) of speech as its causal condition,
one attains seven virtues through the internal power of the middle stage.
Regarding the obstacles to activity:
When one initiates various activities through excessive discursive thought,
thereby agitating the mind and causing the abandonment of the cultivation of wholesome qualities, this is called the "obstruction of activity.
This [state] is free from such an obstruction.
The external power possesses five virtues.
Regarding the persistence of the teaching:
although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the Dharma still remains.
Regarding the phrase "preceded by the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and delight (*ruci*) toward the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*)":
one who wishes to establish a thesis must understand both one's own and others' tenets;
therefore, it says "resolute conviction toward the objects of knowledge."
Furthermore, that which is established according to one's own preference serves as the reason (*hetu*).
Regarding the statement in the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, "preceded by craving" (*tṛṣṇā-pūrvaka*),
the intended meaning is as follows:
Based on past craving as the precursor,
the present body is established and so forth; thus,
the provisional designation of a "sentient being" abides.
The seeds of names and phrases within the activity serve as the primary cause;
the arising of the dharma-entity serves as the establishing agent;
and at the time of arising, the various conditions serve as the harmonious conjunction.
The function of establishing [phenomena] is taken as the fruit.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of the Eighteen [Bases]) states:
"That very same preceding birth serves as the establishment."
The preceding [section] on the conditions for arising as a synthesis and so forth concludes the analysis of establishment, which is divided into three parts.
First, the causal condition is established based on the locus of dependence.
Next, following the explanation of the meaning of causes, conditions, and fruits, there are three subsequent sections that further clarify the establishment of causes.
Regarding the first, which concerns the three bases upon which they depend:
as for the designation of causes—
The substance (*tattva*) is the locus (*āśraya*);
its meaning is termed the "cause" (*hetu*).
Since the meaning is established in dependence upon the substance, it is said that the ten causes depend upon the fifteen loci.
Regarding the term "basis" (*āśraya*):
speech is the cause, which is itself the basis;
this continues up to the point where there is no obstruction, which is also the basis.
All [these] possess their respective functions.
Since they rely upon their bases, they are established as causes;
in accordance with this explanation, they are indeed causes.
Up to the point where non-contradiction itself is the cause,
all of these are also *dharmadhāra* (possessors of their own function). First, regarding the basis (*āśraya*):
Its essence is solely speech;
this speech is called the "reason" (hetu) because it manifests the result, which is the meaning.
As for the statement in the text, "Because it is named first, [it is] perception and so forth," this means that the teaching arises through a gradual sequence: first,
a conventional designation is established collectively for all phenomena— both those bound to and those unbound from the three realms.

In accordance with what is seen, heard, and so forth, when one intends to speak of a phenomenon, one specifically seeks out its name and concept (*saṃjñā*). Because it arises from conceptualization and because it prompts speech, it is so called.
Its basis for apprehension has as its nature that which is depended upon, together with the subject and object of apprehension.
That which is capable of receiving is the category of "receiving," while that which is received consists of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Now, this treatise takes "contemplative dependence" (*apekṣā*) as its cause.
Furthermore, this only clarifies the defiled and the pure,
and thus briefly omits the indeterminate.

The locus of habitual tendencies (vāsanā) has as its intrinsic nature all actual and nominal seeds— whether outflowing (sāsrava) or non-outflowing (anāsrava), internal or external— that are in an unripened state.
This passage explains [the matter] solely in terms of the seeds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
because pure and impure karma induce distinct internal and external results;
it does not explain it in terms of the causes of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) or the purified (*viśuddha*).
The scope of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) is broad and pervasive; it shares the same substance as the moistened seeds and the basis for their support, namely the habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
However, its status in the stage of full accomplishment differs from that which preceded it.
This also refers only to the defiled;
within the defiled, it mentions only karma and not the seeds of names and phrases,
because it follows from what was previously stated.
The basis of the object that has ceased immediately prior within the grasping cause constitutes two conditions.
The faculties refer to the six sense-faculties.
The basis of activity refers to the remaining remote assisting conditions and instruments of action, excluding the causal condition.
The "basis of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-āśraya*) refers to the activity of an agent acting as a direct, manifest condition, excluding causal conditions.
These five [bases] encompass and establish contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Although this is the general discussion, there are distinctions:
If, within the desire realm, the mind and mental factors arise through being sustained by these five kinds of bases as their cause,
whereas if they are material phenomena or formations dissociated from the mind, they arise solely through being sustained by the causal efficiency of their own activity.
Furthermore, "activity" (kāritra) applies broadly to both sentient and insentient things,
whereas "human effort" (puruṣakāra-phala) is narrow, applying only to those included within the category of living beings.
This is the case for the Desire Realm as well as the two higher realms.
The basis of true vision has untainted vision as its intrinsic nature;
excluding that which induces its own seeds,
it assists the associated dharmas.
Subsequently, the untainted [wisdom] can induce [the result],
and it can realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Fully encompassing the six [powers] and discerning the untainted.
Here, the term "or" (hòu) is a word of indefiniteness;
its intent is to show that it does not merely encompass the true vision and the discernment of the untainted.

The "conformity" aspect consists of the seeds and manifestations—both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), which have the nature of being able to induce future existence as their own realm, another realm, or even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruit.
In this text, the term "superior grade" (śreṣṭha-prakāra) excludes those of the same grade or inferior grades.

This is not like the case of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), where acquired wholesome states (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) and defiled states (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) may serve as causes when compared across the nine grades; nor is it like the case of applied wholesome states (*prayoga-labdha-kuśala*), which can serve as causes for those that are equal or superior.
However, because this producing cause (āvāhaka-hetu) is considered in relation to other dharmas, it also functions as a cause;
whereas the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) takes only its own and other [similar] factors as its fruit.
Thus, the functional scope of these two causes varies between being broad and narrow.
Regarding the statement that wholesome dharmas bound to the desire realm can induce those bound to the form and formless realms as well as those that are unbound:

this refers to the stage where the perfections (pāramitās), śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the great bodhisattvas give rise to meditative concentration (dhyāna) and thereby achieve mutual induction and production.
However, as for why the twelfth [verse] mentions only the bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas of the third eon as being able to give rise to all stages (*bhūmi*),
it is said because it refers to arising by spontaneously transcending the stages without relying on effortful application.

Regarding the statement that "indeterminate dharmas can induce the three natures as their conforming basis," this means that while the various seeds may be described as indeterminate when their functional activity is subsumed within their essential nature,
once the cause is attributed to its effect, its nature extends across all three.
Now, based on the principle that functions are subsumed within their nature and that consciousness is of the same nature [as its objects],
it is said that the indeterminate (avyākṛta) induces the three natures.
Apart from this, there is no distinct nature between various manifest phenomena in relation to manifest phenomena, nor between various seeds in relation to seeds.
It constitutes a conforming cause (*anuloma-hetu*).

Its specific functional capacity has as its intrinsic nature the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), based upon this, are able to produce their own respective conditioned effects or realize unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
The nature of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* as a treatise that follows [the sūtras] is narrow,
because it abides in its own essential nature; however,
when discussing the *dhātus*, it is broad.
Because it draws forth [beings] into the three realms,
the nature of this distinction as a basis for treatises is broad;
because it summons maturation (*vipāka*).
To speak of them in terms of their realms is narrow,
for they each belong to their own specific realm and are fixed as distinct.
The preceding [category], being concordant, is considered a non-reliance when compared to the inferior reliance.
This basis of differentiation is obtainable by all;
the basis of integration has as its essence the second basis of experience up to the basis of the functional capacity for differentiation.
Master Ce asked:
"The preceding six causes are sufficient to clarify the meaning;
why is it necessary to establish the cause of 'common purpose' separately?"
Answer: The first six are specific, while "common purpose" is general;
this is because the general and the specific are distinct.
Question: Among the conditions, what is meant by this?
Answer: There are both general and specific types.
Specifically, the three conditions are the specific, while the predominant condition is the general.
However, within the causes themselves there are two types:
first, the brief [classification], which means that the cause of common purpose subsumes the preceding six causes;
second, the extensive [classification], which means that the cause of non-contradiction subsumes the preceding eight causes.
Setting aside contradictory causes,
if one speaks of the four fruits— arising, abiding, accomplishment, and attainment— within the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*),
there are two kinds of accomplishment.
First, the establishment; second, the demonstration.
These [factors] comprise the accomplishment, for without them there would be no functional activity.
"Abiding" refers to the water-mandala resting upon the wind-mandala and so forth.
This is not present in this treatise.
Why do the two treatises differ in what they include and exclude?
It is because the intended purport and the points of reference for the two treatises are distinct.
Since that activity is non-existent apart from its substance,
it is not discussed. Furthermore,
this "non-abiding" is not discussed because it is remote.
The basis of obstruction refers to all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena that can oppose arising and so forth; these constitute its essence.
Question: How can unconditioned phenomena act as obstructions?
The commentary states:
For instance, such things as constructing palaces and the like in dependence upon space cannot be accomplished;
this refers to the meaning of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) acting as an obstructive cause.
Question: What serves as the fruit of this contradiction?
Explanation:
That which causes phenomena not to arise and not to abide, etc., by the power of obstruction, is precisely its fruit.
This means that a future dharma which is about to arise fails to arise because of the presence of an obstacle;
it is not because a dharma already arisen in the present ceases of its own accord.

The basis of non-obstruction refers to those factors that do not obstruct the arising and so forth of phenomena; it takes as its essence all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas in their universal application.
It is established based on the locus of seeds and conditions as the causes and conditions, such as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and others.
Regarding the theory of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), there are two explanations. One states that it refers to the third [of the three types of] habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
The fourth is "possessing moisture," the eleventh is "conformity," and the twelfth is "differentiation."
The thirteenth is harmony;
the fifteenth is non-obstruction.
Among these six bases, all types of causal conditions are collectively termed the "basis of the seed-condition."
Based on this, the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are established.
With the exception of the third and fourth bases, the remaining four bases are not mentioned because their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) have mostly been severed;
alternatively, they are also called "seeds" (*bīja*) because they are capable of producing results.
Regarding "the basis of the immediately preceding cessation as its object," one should understand that this generally indicates the basis of the two conditions;
it does not refer solely to the fifth [condition], the immediately preceding cessation.
Because within the sixth basis for conditions—the objective field—there are also the meanings of the two intermediate conditions;
apart from this, all other locations consist solely of the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Second, it says:
Seeds belong exclusively to the fourth "basis for moistened seeds";
it is based on this that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is established.
Because it is the direct producer of the fruit and its manifestation is evident, it is specifically mentioned here.
The remaining [faculties], such as name and so forth, are omitted from discussion because they are coarse and obscure;
the immediate [condition] pertains only to the fifth [consciousness],
and the objective condition pertains only to the sixth.
Just as in the case of names, which manifest within their own remaining bases,
although these two [types of manifestation] exist, they are not mentioned here because they are implicit;
this has already manifested the first three conditions.
The remaining twelve bases are all comprised within predominance;
it is not merely predominance alone.
