To distinguish the substance of the five fruits:
The ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) has as its essence the indeterminate five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) summoned by all karma;
whether it be a specific retribution or a general one, it is collectively termed "ripening.

The outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) has as its nature the subsequent result produced from a preceding collection of similar, inferior dharmas—whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), tainted (*sāsrava*), or untainted (*anāsrava*), and belonging to any of the three natures (*tridhātu*)—which are of the same category and superior to their cause.
The Yogācāra and Vijñaptimātra schools also state that,
in some cases, subsequent results follow along with what resembles prior karma;
for example, one obtains a short lifespan as a result of killing.
This is the outflow of the designation "superior" (adhipati) in its true sense,
because their short lifespans are identical.

The fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala) has as its nature the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) realized by abandoning the obstacles of afflictions and attaining the fruits [of the path].
The analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained by abandoning the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) and so forth are merely dominant fruits (adhipati-phala),
because the nature of the obstructions abandoned is not a bound phenomenon (saṃyoga-dharma).
Those obtained through the six practices are likewise subsumed under the category of dominant fruits.
Because it does not sever the seeds.
Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), there are two meanings. One says:
The provisional entity of the five aggregates has as its nature the four sense objects obtained through activity.
As it says in [the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*], fascicle 38:
"Because divination and agriculture constitute its intrinsic nature."
The second [master] says:
It has all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena as its nature,
because each and every phenomenon is designated by the name "person" (*pudgala*).
Because this [karma] can bring about four kinds of fruits— namely, the co-arising fruit, the immediate fruit, the non-obstructed fruit, and the distant fruit—
the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala) has all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena as its nature.
Because its nature is expansive and pervasive,
the text states:
"Based on the locus of the conditions that accord with habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one designates the results of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and results of uniform outflow (*niṣyandaphala*)."
The Chinese text corresponding to this passage states: "Consciousness alone is allocated [to these functions]:
the basis of habitual tendencies (vāsanā) obtains the retributive fruit (vipākaphala);
the basis of conformity obtains the concordant fruit (niṣyandaphala)."
Each attains its respective fruit because it possesses a superior capacity; therefore,
they are explained separately.
That which is not a locus of habitual tendencies cannot have an outflow (niṣyanda).
This is the explanation according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Regarding the attainment of these five fruits, there are two interpretations.

One explanation states that "the locus of habitual tendencies" refers to the fact that these five bases— the third, fourth, tenth, twenty-third, and twenty-fifth— obtain the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
As for "the conforming locus":
This indicates that the third, fourth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, thirteenth, fifteenth, or alternatively, the eighth function is taken;
thus, whether eight or nine, these bases obtain their outflow results (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Regarding the "points of true vision," these manifest as the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fifteenth, or the eighth and ninth;
thus, whether five or seven, these various bases attain the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
The basis for the function of the person (puruṣakāra) further has two meanings:
first, the conventional person consisting of the five aggregates;
second, the individual dharmas.
As explained previously regarding the fruits:
according to the first interpretation,
it is shown that these four bases— the second, ninth, thirteenth, and fifteenth— attain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If one follows the latter interpretation,
it clarifies that these ten bases— the second, third, fourth, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, thirteenth, fifteenth, and [the sixteenth]— attain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
As for the remaining locations,

this indicates that the first, fifth, sixth, and fourteenth— these four bases in their entirety— and portions of the remaining eleven as appropriate, obtain the fruit of predominance (*adhipatiphala*).
Because it is what remains after attaining the first four fruits;
otherwise, [the definition] would be either too broad or too narrow.
Second, it is said:
Habitual tendencies (vāsanā) alone, as the third, obtain the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala);
those that are concordant (anuvartin) alone, as the eleventh, obtain the fruit of outflow (niṣyandaphala);
and true vision (samyagdarśana) alone, as the tenth, obtains the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyogaphala).
The "human effort" (puruṣakāra) fruit is obtained solely by the ninth [path];
the remaining eleven obtain the "dominant" (adhipati) fruit.
Each receives its name according to the predominance of its respective meaning.
It is stated that only those who have attained the fruit [of the path] do so, while others do not;
the details are as explained in the treatise.
Next, in the explanation of the meaning:
Question: If "conducive to benefit" constitutes the meaning of a reason (*hetu*),
how can one establish a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*)?
The Master said:
"Because that which is contrary to the dharma is made conducive and beneficial within the context of obstacles,
it may also be said that the meaning of 'conducive and beneficial' is the meaning of 'cause'."
Third, regarding the repeated clarification of the establishment of causes:
the first repetition clarifies the proximity and distance of causes,
while the subsequent repetition clarifies the defilement and purity of causes.
Next, the causes are further elucidated through seven aspects.
Within the first aspect,
the skillful means of productive generation fully encompasses all ten causes.
The remaining three causes are established based on the meanings of the preceding two causes.
Regarding the two explanations of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), one says:
The six causes— namely, attraction (*ākṣepaka*), production (*abhinirvartaka*), leading forth (*āvāhaka*), differentiation (*pratiniyama*), simultaneous activity (*sahabhū*),
and non-contradiction (*avirodha*)— are all termed "productive" (*janaka*) when they exist either as actualities or as seeds and function as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because it directly brings about the fruit,
the remaining four causes and a small portion of the six are all *upāya-hetu* (causes as means),
for they provide indirect assistance in its arising.
Second, it is said:
Only the productive cause is called the "generative cause" (*janakahetu*);
the remaining nine causes are called "expedient causes" (*upāyahetu*).
The arising of the fruit is explained with particular emphasis on its immediate proximity;
it is not solely due to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), but because other conditions provide indirect assistance, they are mentioned with such specific focus.
It is not without causes and conditions;
however, it is stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* that these two seeds— namely, those that project [a future existence] and those that bring about its arising— are called "productive causes."
The remaining skillful means are subsumed therein;
these too have been explained in two ways,
but fearing prolixity, I shall cease here.
In the second section, "Furthermore," it is stated that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is the cause of birth and death;
this consists of the desirable and the undesirable, as well as their increase and their cessation.
This means that even supramundane existence has both the desirable and the increasing.
The desirable and the undesirable are the causes of the branch of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).
As for "increasing," it refers to the increase of the branch of existence consisting of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*).

Alternatively, that which did not previously exist but now exists and is termed "lovely" or "unlovely," and that which previously existed and now encounters moisture, is called the cause of growth (*puṣṭi-hetu*).
Regarding the seven characteristics within the third section:
How do these correspond to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the six characteristics of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)?
It is said that the first characteristic, impermanence, corresponds to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Opening up the second characteristic, being a cause for other-natures (*parabhāva*), corresponds to simultaneous existence (*sahabhū*).
If it were to take its own nature as a cause in the subsequent moment, it would necessarily follow [the entity] constantly.
The third [moment], having already arisen but not yet ceased, establishes the two meanings of "simultaneous existence" (*sahabhū*) and "following" (*anugama*) mentioned previously.
The fourth [moment], upon obtaining other conditions, establishes the fifth meaning: "dependence on a multitude of conditions" (*pratyaya-sāmagrī-apekṣā*).
The fifth, the characteristic of transformation (*vipariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), further elucidates the meaning of the fifth [point], dependence on various conditions (*pratyaya*).
The sixth, the correspondence of functional capacity (*śakti-saṃprayoga*), corresponds to the fourth [point] therein, the determination of nature (*svabhāva-viniścaya*).
The seventh characteristic, that of being appropriate and concordant, corresponds to the sixth [characteristic] mentioned above, which draws forth its own fruit.
The explanation of the first section, the "Gate of the Initial Realm" (*ādyadhātu-mukha*), in this stage is now complete.
Second, regarding the explanation of the characteristics:

Regarding the essential nature of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought): if their nature is defined as volition (*cetanā*) that does not deeply investigate the object, or if their nature were defined as wisdom (*prajñā*) that deeply investigates the object, it would contradict the Abhidharma.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Vitarka and vicāra are, respectively, either volition (cetanā) or wisdom (prajñā), and either investigative deliberation (tarka) or non-investigative deliberation.
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is correct;
one should apply the categories of the *Abhidharma* in reverse order to it.
If there is no deliberation, that is volition (*cetanā*).
Investigation is wisdom;
this constitutes vitarka and vicāra.
When there is no investigation, its nature is simply thought (cetanā).
If, at the time of investigation, both have wisdom as their nature and take the meaning of name-groups (*nāmakāya*) and so forth as their object,
there are two explanations regarding consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
One says: the five consciousnesses also arise together.
Another says: [they do not].
It is associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This text serves as proof;
for it speaks only of taking names and so forth as objects, and does not mention taking visible forms and so forth as objects.
Regarding the phrase "there are seven kinds of distinctions between vitarka and vicāra," the *Wenbei* commentary explains:
"If one follows what is stated here in the text, there are seven kinds of distinctions between vitarka and vicāra."
As explained in the preceding analysis,
one should know that the seven types of mental application (*manopavicāra*) mentioned in the second fascicle all belong to the mental stage (*manobhūmi*).
Among these seven, spontaneous conceptualization (*nirūpaṇa-vikalpa*) refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which takes the same objects as the five sensory consciousnesses.
The seven types of conceptualization associated with volition (*cetanā*) are all distinctions of vitarka and vicāra.

Previously, Master Xuanzang determined that "intrinsic conceptualization" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as it shares its objects of perception with the five sensory consciousnesses.

The later judgment [of the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra] holds that the spontaneous discrimination (*svarasavāhin-vikalpa*) described therein refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which shares the same objects as the five sensory consciousnesses;
this differs from the Abhidharma (Dharma-paryāya),
which maintains that these five consciousnesses constitute the "discrimination by nature" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) among the three types of discrimination.
Alternatively, it has vitarka and vicāra as its essence.
Regarding the position that all vitarka and vicāra are necessarily conceptualizations (vikalpa),
there are two masters in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only).
One interpretation states that "discrimination" (vikalpa) refers exclusively to the defiled [dharmas]; it is the third among the five dharmas.
Therefore, the essential natures of vitarka and vicāra do not extend to the untainted (anāsrava).
A second opinion states that their discrimination extends to the untainted.
Subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) is said to possess conceptualization (*savikalpa*);
thus, its essence—namely vitarka and vicāra—also extends to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
This term "conceptualization" certainly does not refer to the "conceptualization" found among the five dharmas.
Regarding the statement that in the hells (*naraka*), vitarka and vicāra induce suffering associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*),
there are two views among the Vijñānavādins. One says:
The five consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra.
Mental painful sensation is termed "sorrow" (daurmanasya).
This statement regarding the induction of suffering refers to this.
Investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can induce suffering;

it is not said that the five sensory consciousnesses lack investigation and analysis, but rather that investigation and analysis are mentioned specifically in relation to the mental consciousness because its continuity is predominant.
It is associated with sorrow;
it does not exclude being accompanied by suffering,
nor is there any fault in this.
The second [master] says:
"The five consciousnesses are devoid of vitarka and vicāra.
This text serves as the proof.
This can be understood from the text as it stands.
The reason "equanimity" (upekṣā) is not mentioned is that all mental factors (caitta) are necessarily associated with it.
The sensation of mental oppression is in fact the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*);

this case is also like that.

If one were to say that there was previously no [self] and that once perception arose, there subsequently arose various perceptions and so forth—

Regarding the first perception:
the *Aṣṭasaptati* states that it exists in the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Regarding "various perceptions":
this refers to those in the lower stages;

To grasp immeasurable forms as "I" or "mine," and so forth, is called the "immeasurable perception.

According to their respective order, the former two possess the latter two;

or one clings to the view that the self is formless and is reborn after death in a realm of perception.
If one maintains that the self is omnipresent both in the material and the immaterial, being neither dual nor deficient,

therefore, these are omitted here and not discussed.
The second [section], the refutation of the atom (*paramāṇu*), contains five points of critical inquiry.

Regarding the first: "If it has already been examined that [the atom] contradicts the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," this is because it is not apprehended by either of the two means of valid cognition—direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
It is just like a rabbit's horn;
it is certainly not substantially existent,
even though that school claims it is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This school asserts that this is not a cognition based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding distant color (*dūre-rūpa*), only coarse forms larger than an *aṇu* can be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because they are not [composed of] atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The second objection states:
"It is unreasonable to claim that what is increasingly weak and inferior is permanent. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
A subtle transformation that is inferior cannot be permanent,
because it is subject to diminution and weakness, like *naṭa-se-naṭa-se*.
Because he reckons that this coarse form perishes through disintegration;
if it were by way of different characteristics, then the atom would transcend the characteristics of earth, water, and so forth,
as they possess dissimilar characteristics.
It should be unable to produce a fruit of that same category.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: atoms should not possess the characteristics of earth, water, and so forth.
Because it is admitted that water and other elements possess characteristics distinct from their respective bases,
just like the mind and mental factors;
furthermore, they likewise cannot produce effects such as earth.
Because they do not belong to that same category,
just like the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, since no distinct characteristic can be found apart from earth and the other elements, those atoms are certainly not earth and so forth.
Because they do not belong to that category,
like space and so forth;
all these objections herein belong to our own school.
Regarding the third objection:
"If they were not of different characteristics, then because there would be no distinction from their cause, they too should likewise be eternal," etc.
Their original position was as follows:
Because the coarse matter that is produced does not exceed the magnitude of its cause; otherwise,
it would be difficult to maintain that the effect is also eternal, as it would lack any distinct characteristics,
just like its cause.
There is no certainty.
If it were the case that all fruits could arise at all times from dispersed [atoms],
then during the period of world-formation (*vivartakalpa*), when aggregated matter arises from individual dispersed atoms, [this fault would follow].
Then, during the period of the empty eon (*śūnyakalpa*), all atoms (*paramāṇu*) would be capable of producing effects,
because the cause would exist constantly,
just as it does at the time of the formation of an eon (*vivartakalpa*).
It is not only at the time of completion that there is an effect due to a cause;
therefore, the causal relationship lacks a definitive meaning.
This has already been refuted above.
The following refutes the fundamental position:
If one claims that [the effect] does not exceed the dimensions, substance, and qualities of its cause,
then since the two measures of cause and effect are identical in size, [the effect would be indistinguishable from the cause].
What is meant by the atom being called a "substantial part" (*dravyāṃśa*) and possessing a coarse shape with parts?
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The resultant matter produced does not exceed the magnitude of its cause."
It should be understood that, just as an atom is not designated as coarse matter, it serves as the measure;
as stated in the fourteenth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:
If it were not the case that [atoms] do not overlap, then coarse, material objects would be as ungraspable and invisible as atoms, because they would lack material resistance.
Furthermore, it is illogical for non-transparent objects to occupy the same location simultaneously.

Their rebuttal—that because the qualities of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) are conjoined, atoms are not coarse even though they appear coarse, and so forth—is refuted by the same arguments used against them.

Furthermore, if one were to object: "Since the substance of atoms has no subtle parts, it cannot be further analyzed; therefore, the coarse objects produced from them must also be eternal," [the response follows].
The *Xianyang lun* (14) states:
"If one exceeds that measure,
then at the place where the measure is exceeded, coarse, obstructive matter is not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*)."
It must be eternally abiding.
This intention is difficult to explain:
since atoms have no subtle parts and cannot be divided, they are designated as eternal.
In all cases where coarse objects are produced in excess of their measure, the remaining subtle parts cannot be further divided; these too ought to be eternal.
Furthermore, it is difficult [to maintain that] what is produced by the conjunction of two [atoms] is called an "ultimate atom" (paramāṇu).
If you further argue that in those places exceeding the [perceived] magnitude, other subtle parts— namely, single atoms (*paramāṇu*)— arise where they previously did not exist,
then your position is that the atom is permanent.
This is not reasonable, because it is admitted that [the entity] is newly produced.
As the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
Furthermore, if it were admitted that other atoms arise,
then atoms would necessarily be impermanent. Or,
if it were admitted that gross objects are composed of subtle atoms and undergo new arising— coming into existence where they previously did not exist— [the same consequence would follow].
It follows that all atoms must be impermanent;
this objection against the previous position does not exceed the scope of the argument,
for such an over-extension of the argument is merely a counter-argument.
"Not exceeding the measure" is the fundamental tenet of our own school.
What has preceded constitutes the third section of the refutation,
which contains three successive negations.
The meaning can be understood by examining the text.
Regarding the fourth objection,
there are three [points] in the *Xianyang* [Śāstra].
First, if they arise as the same substance as a seed, they should be impermanent;
second, if they arise as the same substance as milk, the atoms should undergo transformation;
third, if they arise as a distinct substance from a potter, then the exertion involved would be a matter of volition.
There are two difficulties in establishing Vijñaptimātratā:
first, the difficulty regarding atoms;
second, the difficulty regarding gross matter.
The atom faces three difficulties:
first, it is a real entity;
second, it is eternal.
Third, regarding the capacity to produce:
there are two difficulties concerning coarse matter (*audārika-rūpa*).
First, it does not exceed the dimensions of its cause.
Second, they are substantially existent;
all these points are as detailed in that [text].
Regarding the fifth objection:
Furthermore, who could possibly restrict their functional capacity?
Who could restrict the power of sentient beings within the atoms so as not to allow them to arise?
This can be known through inference.
If it is said that external objects arise not by depending on sentient beings, then they would arise without purpose.
"Purpose" (yòng) here means "by means of" (yóu). [External objects] would have no purpose with respect to sentient beings.
It is not logical that external objects arise independently of sentient beings.
The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:
External objects such as you [assert] should not arise,
because they would be useless for sentient beings,
like the hair of a tortoise and so forth.
In these fetters, there are eight instances of the character "hence" (故).
The first three fetters refute the forty views of eternalism;
the latter five fetters refute the notion that atoms are eternal.
Regarding "because they share common characteristics":
permanence and impermanence share common characteristics. Regarding "because of their own characteristics": [the following applies].
Because the characteristics of difference and non-difference are its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the second point, the presentation of the correct meaning, Ji says:
"At all times" refers to the three periods of time.
"In every way" refers to among all the various categories of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
"Spontaneously" refers to its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).
That which is destroyed by another is a perishable thing;
that which is unarisen has no origination.
Among these five, that which is neither subject to change nor movement is called "permanent."
That which was previously calculated by him contradicts these five points;
it is clearly known that they are impermanent and should not be falsely clung to.
To explain further now:
The first two phrases speak of the characteristic of non-alteration in contrast to alteration.
Regarding "at all times and in all ways," this is the explanation of Master Tongji (Sthiramati).
The latter three phrases should be explained as being without change:
that which is spontaneous is the characteristic of space;
that which is due to others is the characteristic of analytical cessation.
That which is unarisen is the characteristic of cessation through non-analytical discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
